title: Choosing Form and Tone for Your Audience
keyIdea: Before writing, ask who the audience is and what the purpose is: to inform, persuade, entertain or instruct. The purpose points to a form (a letter, report, set of instructions, review or story), and the audience sets the tone and the vocabulary. The same message can be written chatty for a friend, polite for a teacher and very formal for a council, and the same facts can be told in easier words for a younger reader. A line in the wrong tone or the wrong form makes the whole piece work less well.

kid: Writers make choices before they start. They ask two questions. Who is my audience, the person who will read this? And what is my purpose? The four big purposes are to inform (give facts), persuade (get someone to agree or act), entertain (make them enjoy it) and instruct (tell them how to do something).

The purpose helps you pick the form, the kind of text. Want the head teacher to say yes to a bike rack? Write a letter. Sharing facts about birds? A report, with headings. Showing how to fold a paper plane? Instructions, with numbered steps and bossy verbs like fold and press. Saying if a film is good? A review, with your opinion and a rating. Want to make people laugh? Try a story.

The audience sets the tone. Tone is how the writing sounds, from chatty to very formal. A note to your best friend can say “Hi! Can we use the hall on Friday?” A letter to the town council needs “Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to ask whether we may use the hall on Friday.” Same message, different reader, different tone.

The audience also changes your words. For a 6-year-old, “Precipitation descends from cumulonimbus clouds” becomes “Rain falls from huge storm clouds.” The facts stay. When you check your work, look for lines that do not fit, like “lol” in a letter to the head, or “Once upon a time” in a letter asking for something.
adult: This matches the upper Key Stage 2 writing goals in the English national curriculum. In Years 5 and 6, pupils should plan by identifying the audience for and purpose of the writing and by selecting the appropriate form. They should also select vocabulary and grammar to suit, and recognise how formal speech and writing differ from informal. In the US, Common Core W.4.4 and W.5.4 ask for writing whose development and organisation suit the task, purpose and audience. L.4.3c and L.5.3 cover choosing formal or informal English by context.

A few terms help. Purpose is why the text exists; teachers often use the four broad purposes inform, persuade, entertain and instruct. Form, or text type, is the shape that serves it: letter, report, instructions, review, story. Each has features children can name, such as numbered steps and imperative verbs in instructions. Tone is the attitude the text sounds like. Register, or level of formality, is a big part of tone. Lesson 185 practises the formal and informal word swaps; this lesson adds purpose, form and writing for a younger reader.

Common mistakes to watch for: naming the topic when asked for the purpose (it is about bikes, rather than it is to persuade); picking a form by habit, so everything becomes a story; opening a letter to an official with Hiya or text speak; thinking formal is always best, so a note to a friend sounds stiff; making text for a younger reader easier by dropping the facts instead of swapping hard words; and mixing forms in one piece, such as a Step 1 list inside a persuasive letter.

In the lab your child names the purpose of four writing tasks and drags five tasks onto the form that fits. They slide a tone dial until one message suits a best friend, a teacher and the town council. They swap hard words so two science sentences work for a 6-year-old, and find three lines in a letter to the head that break its tone or form. The Challenge mixes all of these, with a hint for each wrong choice.

familyTip: Pick one small piece of news, like a lost cat or a school fair. Write it three ways together: a text to a friend, a poster for the village hall and a letter to the local paper. Then read them aloud and ask: what changed, and why did it need to?

visual.caption: Chatty or formal? Drag each opening, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name the purpose, pick the form, set a tone dial for three readers, simplify for a 6-year-old and spot lines that do not fit.

practice.prompt: You write to ask the head teacher for a longer lunch break. What is your purpose?
practice.hint: What do you want the head to do after reading it?
practice.explain: You want the head to agree and act, so the purpose is to persuade.

practice.prompt: Your instructions have {n} steps. Each step starts with one bossy verb. How many bossy verbs are there?
practice.hint: One bossy verb, like fold or press, at the start of each step.
practice.explain: {n} steps with one imperative verb each gives {n} bossy verbs.

practice.prompt: A report has {h} headings with {f} facts under each. How many facts is that?
practice.hint: Each heading has the same number of facts. Multiply.

practice.prompt: Which form fits “How to look after a goldfish”?
practice.hint: Does the reader need steps to follow?
practice.explain: The reader needs to know what to do, in order, so instructions with numbered steps fit best.

pool.prompt: Which opening suits a letter to the town council?
pool.hint: The council is an official audience you do not know.
pool.explain: A formal audience needs a formal opening: Dear Sir or Madam.

pool.prompt: Your reader is 6. Which sentence suits them best?
choices: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.
Bees facilitate pollen transfer between flowers.
pool.hint: Keep the facts, but use easy words.
pool.explain: Easy words and the same facts. “Facilitate” is too hard, and “lol” drops the facts.

pool.prompt: What is the purpose of a joke book?
pool.explain: Jokes are there to make the reader enjoy it and laugh, so the purpose is to entertain.

pool.prompt: Which line does NOT fit a letter asking the head for a bike rack?
choices: Many of us cycle to school.
Please could we have one by summer?
pool.hint: Which line belongs to a different form?
pool.explain: Numbered steps belong in instructions. The letter's purpose is to persuade.

pool.prompt: A review of a new game should include…
pool.hint: What makes a review different from a report?
pool.explain: A review tells the reader what you thought and why, often with a rating.

pool.prompt: A tone dial goes from 0 (very chatty) to 4 (very formal). It is on {d}. The council needs 4. How many clicks towards formal?
pool.hint: Each click moves the dial up by one. Count on from {d} until you reach 4.
pool.explain: From {d} up to 4 is {=4-d} clicks towards formal.

choices: No, it depends on the audience
pool.hint: How would a very formal text to your best friend sound?
pool.explain: Formal suits officials and strangers. To a friend, chatty fits better. Match the tone to the reader.

pool.prompt: Mia is asked for the purpose of her bike-rack letter. She says “It is about bikes.” What did she give?
pool.hint: Purpose is why you write, not what it is about.
pool.explain: Bikes are the topic. The purpose is to persuade the head to say yes.

pool.prompt: A sentence for a 6-year-old has {w} words. You swap {n} hard words for easy ones. How many words is it now?
pool.hint: A swap takes one word out and puts one word in.
pool.explain: Each swap is one word for one word, so it still has {w} words. Only the hard words changed.
